title: I finally remade my childhood game thanks to Claude!
author: Odd-Childhood1824
selftext:
Hey everyone!

I've been working on Line Racer, an arcade racing game where you draw your own racing line and try to master each track through precision, speed, and timing.

This is a passion project I've been developing solo alongside my full-time work. The game is now playable on ANDROID only, and I'm continuing to add new tracks, features, improvements, and optimizations as development goes on.

I'm sharing it here because I'd really love some honest feedback:  
\- Does the drawing mechanic feel intuitive?  
\- Does the gameplay look satisfying?  
\- What would you improve or add?

If you try it, I'd genuinely appreciate any feedback, bug reports, or ideas. Every suggestion helps shape the future of the game.

Thanks for checking it out!

AI disclosure:  
This game was developed with heavy assistance from AI tools. I am not a professional programmer, so I used AI as a coding partner to help build and debug systems while I focused on the game design, mechanics, visuals, level design, and overall direction.

The concept, gameplay decisions, track design, and final creative choices are mine. AI was used as a development assistant throughout the process.

replies.author: Odd-Childhood1824
replies.body:
For now, I want to keep it completely free to play and focus on building an active player base. The more people playing, the better the feedback, and the better I can make the game.

If I ever monetize it, I'd much rather do it through content than ads. My current idea is something like keeping **Sector A** free, then charging around **€3** to unlock the rest of the game (new sectors/maps), almost like a small DLC. I really don't want ads in the game, they tend to break the flow, and that's something I want to avoid.

I'm also planning an iOS release once I reach around **1,000+ Android downloads** and have polished the game a bit more.

Steam was actually part of the original plan too, but after testing, I realized the game just feels much better on a touchscreen. Drawing smooth racing lines with a mouse is possible, but it's noticeably less natural and less fun. During PC testing I only had three testers, and while it was definitely playable, everyone agreed it was much more enjoyable on a phone or tablet.

So right now my goal isn't really making money, it's finding enough players to validate the concept and keep improving it. If I can build a small but dedicated community that enjoys chasing leaderboard times, I'll consider that a success.

replies.author: Odd-Childhood1824
replies.body:
Thanks! I actually thought a lot about power-ups and car tuning, but I'm struggling to find a way to implement them without going against the core idea of the game.

For example, if I place a power-up at a specific spot on the track, players who want the best times will feel forced to draw their line through that point. The whole concept of the game is that you're free to draw your own racing line, and different lines lead to different results. Fixed power-ups would reduce that freedom.

Random power-ups have another problem. Once you unlock Gold Medal on a track, the game becomes very competitive, and it's important that every player races on exactly the same track under the same conditions. I have to be careful with randomness because I don't want one run to be faster than another just because a power-up happened to spawn in the right place. Otherwise, players would end up waiting for the "perfect" RNG instead of improving their driving.

I had similar thoughts about car tuning. Right now, everyone has the exact same car, just like in a competitive game where skill is the deciding factor. If a new player races against someone with better upgrades, that could feel pretty frustrating.

The game isn't really designed around long-term progression through upgrades. At first it can be played casually, but pretty quickly it becomes about mastering the same track, finding the fastest line, and climbing the leaderboard through practice.

That said, I'm definitely open to ideas. If there's a way to add power-ups or customization without hurting the competitive nature of the game, I'd genuinely love to hear it!

replies.author: Odd-Childhood1824
replies.body:
As for different cars, my current approach is to offer different driving modes instead of upgrades.

The standard mode is **Speedster**, and I've already made a first version of a **Drifter** mode. It's the same track, but with completely different handling and a boost button, so it almost feels like learning a new game.

I think that's a better fit for the competitive nature of the game because everyone still has access to the exact same vehicle in each mode, it's all about skill, not upgrades.

Right now it's still a bit unclear though. You need to earn at least a **Diamond medal** on a track to unlock Drifter mode, and I'm still experimenting with whether that's the best way to introduce it.

comments.author: smallfried
comments.body:
Downloaded it, played it. Looks very polished. No bugs encountered.

I wasn't really sure how I could improve the paths I drew and how exactly drawing speed would affect driving speed. Is it capped to a max speed, but if I draw slower it would brake a bit? I guess I wasn't hooked so probably it's not really the game for me.

Played two levels and then uninstalled again. 

Thank you for the experience.

replies.author: Odd-Childhood1824
replies.body:
Thank you so much for taking the time to download it and write such detailed feedback! I really appreciate it.

I'm especially happy to hear you didn't run into any bugs.

Your comment about not understanding how to improve is actually very helpful. You're definitely not the only player who stops after a couple of races. The game is meant to be about gradually mastering the mechanics and finding faster lines, but if that isn't clear early on, it's hard to get hooked. Once it clicks, beating your own ghost and eventually overtaking the gold car almost every race becomes a really satisfying dopamine hit.

The drawing speed controls your car's target speed. Drawing slower makes the car slow down and grip better through corners, while drawing faster lets it carry more speed (up to the car's limit). On top of that, the game heavily rewards drawing smooth, flowing lines instead of sharp turns, and using your boost at the right moments during the race can make a huge difference.

The strategy really begins while you're drawing. I wanted it to feel a bit like thinking as a real racing driver: where can you cut a corner, where should you sacrifice entry speed for a better exit, where is it worth braking a little more to gain speed afterward? The challenge is finding the fastest racing line before the race even starts, then executing it well with your boost timing.

I actually have gameplay tips cycling in the terminal window before each race, but maybe they're not clear or noticeable enough. Looking back, I think I need to do a much better job of teaching these mechanics in-game instead of expecting players to figure them out.

Out of curiosity, do you think a better tutorial or more visual feedback would have made you want to keep trying, or do you feel the core gameplay just isn't for you? Either answer is genuinely useful for me.

Thanks again for giving it a shot!

replies.author: smallfried
replies.body: I have the attention span of a 3 year old with racing games so I'm probably not the right public. I probably wouldn't read a longer tutorial. My confusion came from knowing what is fast and slow drawing. I could draw the circuit in a second or take a minute to do it, but what is the drawing speed that corresponds with the fastest driving speed and what is the lower limit where grip is basically maximum? I don't know, maybe some crazy color coding, like a clear quick switch to some specific color when the maximum is reached so you know drawing faster doesn't do anything.

replies.author: Odd-Childhood1824
replies.body:
That's actually a really interesting point, and I think I understand where the confusion comes from now.

It sounds like you assumed the drawing speed maps directly to the car's speed, almost like you're controlling the throttle yourself. That's actually not how the system works, and I think that's on me for not explaining it well enough.

The line you draw is more like giving instructions to your "AI driver" than directly driving the car. You're basically saying, "go full throttle here," "slow down for this corner," or "take this racing line." The car still reacts based on its own physics, grip, momentum, and the situation it's in. So drawing faster isn't about hitting some exact speed value—it's more like telling the AI to be more aggressive, while drawing slower tells it to be more cautious.

I think I accidentally gave players the impression that they need to find the "perfect drawing speed," when the real challenge is making good racing decisions: finding a smooth racing line, cutting corners where possible, carrying speed through exits, and using boost at the right moments.

Your comment made me realize I probably need to rethink how I explain the mechanic entirely. So thanks again, that was genuinely insightful.
